subtopic: P.O. DEPARTMENT LOSSES ON SECOND CLASS MAIL
speechtext:
1. Information on which to estimate the deficit for 1963 is not yet available.
2.	Information for the last ten years is not available. The department has recognized for some time, particularly since the release of the Glassco report, that the statistical data being maintained was insufficient to give the necessary information relative to second class mail posted in the United States for delivery in Canada. During the past year the department has engaged in an extensive study as to required statistics covering the entire postal field, and recently the services of management consultants were engaged to assist in these studies.
For the year 1961-62 information has been obtained from the United States administration as to the volume of second class mail posted in that administration for delivery in Canada. By using this information, together with statistics compiled in this department, it is estimated that the deficit for handling second class mail from the United States for delivery in Canada during 1961-62 is $3,900,000 divided as follows: (a) on second class mail posted in the United States for delivery in Canada, $2,800,000; (b) on United States second class mail posted in Canada for delivery in Canada, $1,100,000.

May I speak briefly on this motion at this time. This motion is for the production of copies of telegrams and other correspondence exchanged between the C.B.C. and individuals or organizations in connection with the conversion of Toronto radio station CJBC from an English station to a French station. I am informed by the C.B.C. that a total of 1,904 letters have been received in this connection. If the C.B.C. were to comply with the motion as it now reads it would require the duplication of over 3,800 communications representing a total of approximately 5,000 pages. speechtext:

Order, please. I think it is my duty to bring to the attention of the hon. member citation 152 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, paragraph 4, and with the permission of the house I will read it:
(4) All references to judges and courts of justice and to personages of high official station, of the nature of personal attack and censure, have always been considered unparliamentary, and the Speakers of the British and Canadian houses have always treated them as breaches of order. Members have even been interrupted in committees of the whole by the chairman when they have cast an imputation upon a judicial proceeding. The proper course for persons who feel called upon to attack the conduct of a judge is to proceed by way of a petition in which all the allegations are specifically stated so that the person accused may have full opportunity to answer the charges presented against him.

Mr. Speaker, when I put a question to the Minister of Justice a moment ago you rightly ruled that a member of the house could not attack a judge. But I did not lodge any accusation against Judge Meunier; I only made a reference to an official report published and issued by Judge Wagner of Montreal. And that is why I asked the Minister of Justice whether he intended to suspend Judge Meunier in the light of that official report issued by another judge of Montreal.

Order. I did not refer to this citation before but it is a further citation in Beauchesne. Citation 149 reads in part as follows:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 35 it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada that a member, while speaking, must not:
(c) refer to any matter on which a judicial decision is pending;-

(j) cast reflections upon the conduct of judges of superior courts, unless such conduct is based upon a substantive motion.

Mr. Chairman, while the regular estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration come before the house for discussion, I shall have an opportunity to make an over-all statement on the immigration policy to be carried out by the department.
However, to reply more specifically to the question asked by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), I may say that in accordance with the announcement I made, the immigration policy of the department will be changed.
Nevertheless, I might state briefly what happened in that field. In the past, we had a considerable number of applications from European immigrants wishing to come to Canada, and that raised many problems. I would call that the post-war period which was one of passivity, where we only had to make a selection among the immigrants asking us to come here. As a matter of fact, our problems, at that time, were different from the ones facing us now. We have reached the point where the needs of the country, as regards immigration, are so acute that our immigration policy must be revised and made more positive. There are a few points I want to bring up under these estimates concerning our own native people of Canada. It has been suggested by some that perhaps these native people require their own member of parliament, something like they had in England for the universities, but because they have been neglected for many years the Indians have lost faith in the ability of our parliamentary system to look after their rights. As I say, they have suggested at times that they do require direct representation here in Ottawa. I am sure that the appointment of Mr. Gladstone to the Senate did a great deal for the morale of the Indian people across Canada, who now feel they have some voice in their own affairs.
They are looking ahead, now. They have some hope. But it is certainly not enough, and I do not think this is the real answer. I do think it is the duty of members having Indian reserves in their constituencies-and I have some seven Indian reserves in my district-to bring these matters to the attention of parliament. First, and most important, we must make it clear, once and for all, that we


are playing ball with these people, that they are not being neglected. One of the most vital steps in this connection is the setting up as soon as possible of the Indian claims commission, and giving the Indians a direct connection with it and with the courts and other legal machinery in Canada, so that not only present claims but breaches of the treaty in the past may be looked into. I do not intend to discuss this matter at any length because it has already been brought to the attention of the committee. Anyway, it is a field in which the Indians are looking for some action.
I think the Indian people are essentially no different from any other people. They feel they are being treated as second-class citizens of some kind. Speaking from my own experience I can say they have been treated by the government as if they were children. They are not, in fact, children. Where the Indians have kept their self-respect, and been allowed to keep it, they have shown that in their own way they are very effective Canadian citizens indeed. I would point to the Caughnawaga Indians along the St. Lawrence river. These men are recognized in the United States as being the finest steel workers in America. In fact, they get better wages than the white men employed in this work, because of their greater skill.
In the western reserves, the Bloods and the Peigans in southern Alberta are well off financially. They have never been taken from their original habitat; they live on roughly the same ground as did their ancestors and they have turned successfully to the way of life nearest to that of their ancestors in the days of the buffalo. They are trying to go into ranching. Only recently a delegation came to Ottawa and offered to capitalize their ranches by purchasing breeding stock on a 50-50 basis. They came to the federal government with an offer to put up 50 per cent of the capital cost. Let us not turn this down. Here is a progressive tribe whose members are trying to do something for themselves. They are showing that they have not lost their old grit. Before the white men came they were a fine, upstanding race of people with a keen sense of democracy and a well thought out and stable religious life, all of which has been upset by our well-meaning interference. I suggest we should consult the Indian people and find out how they want to live; and when they come forward with such a manly proposition as supplying 50 per cent of the capital they require, I think we should almost write a blank cheque. For every dollar they put up we have got to meet them.
If they succeed, as they are succeeding in southern Alberta, I should like to ask your co-operation, Mr. Chairman, and the co-operation of this committee in seeing that the

less favoured tribes in my district who may want to do something along these lines should receive every encouragement. I do not expect the department to do all the work.
I do not expect the Indians to do all the work. I intend to make up a party of Indians from my district and take them this summer to visit their cousins on the Blood and Peigan reserves to see how this is working out-to see whether they cannot devote as much energy and courage to building up a venture of this sort. I know it will work. I know these people. I have worked with them, and they are no different, when given a chance, from any other Canadians. It is a question of morale. It is also a question of common sense. We must try to give these people jobs in this country which are as close to their instincts and to their culture as we can. We hear a great deal about biculturalism. Both the English and the French in Canada are proud of their cultures, and there is no doubt at all that the red man is proud of his. He will fit into the Canadian pattern of culture as far as he himself wants to fit in. At one time the white people of this country hoped that the natives would die out. They are not dying out; they are multiplying quite rapidly. This will present an increasing challenge if we do not take steps to meet it and give these people the opportunities which I think they should have.
As a lesser suggestion I think we should improve their morale by paying them their treaty money in cash, as they have requested on many occasions. I suggest we pay them in special money. I suggest we should provide every year special silver dollars honouring the various tribes in the order in which they signed the treaty, and that we pay these senior citizens of ours in Canada in silver money struck especially to honour their people. The details could easily be worked out and I shall not take up the time of the committee in pursuing this matter further, now. But the feeling of the Indians, when they signed this treaty originally, was that they were to be paid in cash in the Queen's money and I believe we could combine the keeping of this part of the treaty with a gesture in honour of those fine Indian tribes who signed it and who have kept their side of the bargain.
Now I wish to turn for a few moments to the subject of old people's homes. In Alberta, we have old folks homes, but there are none for Indians and I suggest we might work out some scheme, in co-operation with the provinces, in order that our aged Indians might also have the benefit of old folks homes. Perhaps they would not require exactly the same type of architecture as we ourselves find suitable. Perhaps provision should be made

But aged Indians who are in receipt of old age pensions might well make the same deal for living in these old folks homes as do our own senior citizens, and they could be looked after in these homes in the same way as we look after the white people. The Indian people have always looked after the aged of their own race. They honour their fathers and their mothers in the same way as we do. If hon. members of this committee came to my district and saw the slums in which the senior citizens of our senior people are living, they would be horrified. I could take them around to mud floored shacks and primitive log dwellings in which these older people are obliged to spend the declining years of their lives in poverty, living under conditions which it is hard to imagine until they have actually been witnessed.
I think we need to do more, too, to train the younger people to take advantage of the mechanical age in which we live. These Indian people are clever mechanics. I understand that if an Eskimo is given an outboard motor he scarcely requires any instruction in its working; he will pull it apart, see how it works and put it together again; he learns the mechanics of an outboard motor much faster indeed than does a white man, because it is essential to his way of life-he has to keep his canoe running so as to carry on his trapping. I am told by my former mates in the police that an Eskimo can beat our boys every time when it comes to mechanical things. So let us see they get the training they require. It is not good enough simply to set up schools where ordinary subjects are taught. We have to provide for the development of this natural mechanical aptitude and teach subjects which have practical application to the kind of life the students want to lead. They are still pioneers. They have the right to live in a pioneer country. I am sure that the undertaking to educate the Indians did not mean teaching them only reading, writing and arithmetic. We must enable them to receive the same training as we give to our own young people, to prepare them for the mechanical age in which we live.
Now I wish to change the subject radically and speak for a few moments about immigration.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it is a matter of great importance that this opportunity be taken to discuss fully in the house a serious question that has been simmering for many months and is now threatening to explode as the result of certain happenings in the last month or so. I am speaking now of the proposed transfer of the jurisdiction over and administration of the affairs of the Eskimo people of northern
[The Deputy Chairman.]
Quebec from the federal government to the government of the province of Quebec. I rise to make some comments and to offer some suggestions and I do so in an objective, sincere and non-partisan manner because this issue is at present very badly confused.
There is growing alarm among southern Canadians and I can assure the house that the Eskimo people of the north are becoming frightened and confused. I think it is important that someone who knows the Eskimo people clarify the record at this stage before the issue becomes clouded by religious and political emotionalism.
This matter has far reaching implications, containing as it does problems of federal-provincial relationships, constitutional questions and the rights of parliament itself but, most important, the fundamental right of a large group of Eskimo Canadian citizens to be, if you will, masters in their own igloos. I suggest that the way in which we approach this problem and ultimately resolve it, as we will, will be under close scrutiny in all parts of Canada and in many other nations of the world because Canada at last will have had to come face to face with a matter that has all the elements of the struggle of emerging people and groups for self-determination.
I regret very much that the Prime Minister is ill and absent from the house today and also that the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources are not here this afternoon because they are the ones who have been carrying on the negotiations respecting this matter with the government of the province of Quebec.
I do not intend to rehash the rather ragged events of some of the question periods on this very issue, except to say that at this point the House of Commons has been told certain things. We know for certain, and we have the Prime Minister's word for it, that the Eskimos are to be consulted before an agreement is signed. Ostensibly that consultation will be carried out through a federal-provincial commission. We know that for sure.
We have also been assured by the Prime Minister that any agreement the federal government signs will safeguard the language and the religion of the Eskimo people of new Quebec. But there are some things we do not know. We have not been told about them in the house and the people of Canada must know before we can proceed any further. We do not know yet whether parliament will have an opportunity to approve or reject any plan that is arrived at. We do not know whether the Eskimo people of new Quebec will have the opportunity to be consulted about the terms of the agreement and to be

represented at any such negotiations by independent counsel. We do not know for sure whether the Eskimo people of northern Quebec will be allowed to have a referendum. We do not know for sure whether similar negotiations will be conducted with regard to Eskimo people who live in other provinces of Canada.
Let me advise the house, in case hon. members do not know, that there are other provinces of Canada that have Eskimo people living in them. The obvious example is the province of Manitoba. There is a substantial Eskimo settlement at Churchill. We do not know what the implications of this move are for the administration of Indian affairs throughout Canada, not only in terms of every province of Canada but in those very communities in the north where Eskimo, Indian and white people have been, until now at least, living in harmony. I give as examples the communities of Great Whale River in new Quebec, Fort Churchill in Manitoba and Inu-vik in the Northwest Territories.
I have said there is growing alarm in southern Canada. One need only read the various newspaper editorials that have appeared on this very matter in recent weeks. I have in my hand a press report of a speech given by the Right Rev. E. S. Reed, Bishop of Ottawa. This is from the Ottawa Citizen for March 12, and I quote from part of the article because Bishop Reed is very concerned over what is happening to the Eskimo people:
Bishop Reed deprecated the fact that, apparently, the Quebec Eskimos jurisdictional problem has become "a highly charged political issue."
Bishop Reed posed these questions in his speech:
Will the good work begun, however, belatedly, by the northern affairs department, be continued and improved if jurisdiction is given to the Quebec government?
Will the missionaries, the trusted friends of the Eskimos, with no political axe to grind, be permitted to assist the Eskimos when their wishes are being consulted on the jurisdictional problem?
I have said, Mr. Chairman, that the Eskimo people are confused. I say this because in recent weeks I have had an opportunity of meeting and talking with the Eskimo people from northern Quebec. I can assure you, as a result of these person to person talks, that the Eskimo people are extremely alarmed about what is occurring between the federal and provincial governments. One of the Eskimo people from Fort Chimo, a man who is completely reliable, assured me that these frightened people will probably pack up and move away from Quebec mainland if this thing proceeds any further without their being allowed to participate in the discussion.
I say that there has been alarm in southern Canada as a result of some of the statements we have seen in the press, statements Mr. Chairman that are unbelievable in their colonial attitude toward the Eskimo people.

Resources minister Rene Levesque, who has pressed Ottawa hard to transfer administrative authority for the Eskimos to Quebec has flatly rejected any idea of a referendum on the grounds that the Eskimos have not reached the cultural stage where they are capable of rendering an opinion, and that a referendum would be accordingly "an abuse of the democratic process".

Interim Supply
we, as a party, support. Let that be understood. There has never been any doubt about where the Conservative party stood on this matter. The objective of having provincial governments assume responsibility for Eskimo and Indian affairs is one that we support. In fact, it is the only way, we believe, you can build a nation. However, the method by which this is achieved is something that causes us alarm.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice, who I see has resumed his seat, that whatever methods are followed in this transfer they must guarantee that the rights of parliament will be respected and that the rights of the Eskimo people to be consulted will be safeguarded. A few days ago in this house the Prime Minister said that no one needed to tell him about his responsibilties. With due respect and deference to our Prime Minister, I suggest there are many things he does need to be told about the Eskimo people. Furthermore, I suggest to him that I am quite competent in this field to tell him a few things that he might not know about the Eskimo people.
I have said that there are constitutional difficulties involved here because a number of these matters are assigned by the British North America Act to federal and provincial jurisdictions. I do not intend to refer to these in any detail. There is a constitution problem involved as a result of the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912 which says in the pertinent section, section 2 paragraph (e):
That the trusteeship of the Indians in the said territory, and the management of any lands now or hereafter reserved for their use, shall remain in the government of Canada subject to the control of parliament.
Certainly the supreme court decision of 1939, which is the basis upon which these negotiations are being conducted between the Minister of Justice and the Quebec government, was to the effect that for the purposes of the British North America Act Eskimos are considered to be Indians. This is surely the most serious part of the current negotiations. The minister, as he indicated in the house, proposes to transfer Eskimo affairs in Quebec from the federal government, and is he going to transfer Indian affairs as well? If he does not, he will have been guilty of building a wall between two racial groups in northern Quebec, particularly those communities where Indians and Eskimos are living at the present moment side by side in harmony.
The Prime Minister has built an image of himself. I believe this image to be an honest one of understanding the need to unite the various racial groups in Canada. He has said he wishes to bind the wounds between the

races. I believe in this, but I suggest that the present agreement which has been reached will do precisely the opposite.
I also suggest that the problem of the jurisdiction over these Eskimo people is essentially the problem of confederation. Heaven knows, the Prime Minister took the time in his fireside talk to the nation to tell us confederation itself was at a crossroads.
I have listened at great length during the question period when this matter was discussed. To date I have not participated in the debate nor have I asked questions about the Eskimo people in northern Quebec. However I do feel the time has come for me to put on the record some of what I know about the Eskimo people and their feelings. The Eskimo people in the Canadian north know me, and know me well. They trust me because I have travelled among them, I have worked among them and I have lived with them. My family has been in the Northwest Territories since the early 1900's. My own children were born in the Northwest Territories, and I know the Eskimo people for all of their qualities. For this reason I want to put on the record some arguments to contradict those things that have been said to date about them.
I recall very well being a resident of the north when the Nielsen bill to extend the federal franchise came before the house. I know the results of that bill were felt locally. They were felt nationally and indeed internationally. At this stage I want to put on the record a quotation that should be of interest to all hon. members, a quotation from a man who conducted the enumeration along the distant early warning line. It is interesting, because it tells about the effect of the vote among American people serving in the Canadian north. I quote:
It was surprising the amount of interest shown on the D.E.W. line in respect of the election. Prior to this they used to do a lot of moaning and criticizing of the government, with the usual remark of "taxation without representation." You never hear the remarks or criticism any more, as just the fact that they can vote in a federal election has resulted in building up the prestige of this wonderful Canada of ours, tremendously in their eyes.. .Believe that the steps taken to bring the vote to the D.E.W. line stations and adjacent villages brought home to our American friends up here the fact that not only is Canada a democracy but that the government is prepared to go to all kinds of trouble and expense to see that Canadian citizens of high and low status, are given an opportunity to vote and elect whatever government representatives that they so desire.
That was a quotation from a letter sent to Mr. Castonguay, and I feel it should be on the record because it shows this measure did have international repercussions.
Some people may ask, do the Eskimo people exercise the franchise they won after so

many years? One need only look at the statistics. The average turn-out at the polls among Eskimo people has been around 79 per cent to 80 per cent of the eligible voters. I personally know of instances where Eskimo families travelled three days and three nights in weather down to 45 degrees below zero, in order to get to the nearest polling station to cast their ballots. If this is not a group of people prepared to assume the responsibility to vote and who are willing and able to be consulted, then I know of no other group like them in Canada.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, to the Minister of Justice and to the minister of northern affairs that these people would be hurt and insulted if we allowed this agreement to take place without their participation.
In conclusion I want to quote a paragraph from some testimony which was given before the standing committee on mines, forests and waters last December by Mr. Robert Williamson. Mr. Williamson is the foremost Eskimo linguist in Canada, and is known to all the Eskimo people throughout the Canadian north as Bob. He speaks all their dialects. He too knows and understands their problems and this is what he said, referring to the Eskimo people:
This is a people who in a very short historical period conquered and successfully lived in the most difficult and merciless part of the world. They covered an area 4,000 miles wide from Alaska to eastern Greenland and extending from as far south as 600 miles north of Ottawa to 500 miles from the pole. All this was done with no resources other than the skins and bones of the country's hard-won game, and the great powers of endurance and resourcefulness of this exceptionally intelligent race. To survive in the north, one had to be intelligent. The less intelligent were simply eliminated by nature. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my brief remarks on such a ticklish question as that of the boundaries between the province of Quebec and the province of Newfoundland, I say right now to the house that I do not pretend to be an expert.
However, as representative of the Saguenay county, which has the largest surface area in Canada, except the Northwest Territories, because it comprises 375,000 square miles and contains a wealth of natural resources, specially iron ore, it is imperative that I say a few words. This county borders on several points of the province of Newfoundland, as varied as they are difficult.
I should also add that the railway line which stretches out from Seven Islands to Schefferville crosses the border into Newfoundland at several points. I often did it on foot and even with snowshoes.
Quebec-Newfoundland Boundary
Again last fall, when I was in Blanc-Sablon, the terminal point of the Quebec Labrador coast, I was quite astonished to see an ordinary rock, bearing no inscription, thrown there haphazardly, as it were, indicating the frontier between the two provinces.
Mr. Speaker, there is no official dividing line between the two provinces. This is not a new problem. It has been the subject of many an article, but to no avail unfortunately.
I think that instead of setting up a committee to consider the matter of frontiers in this vast territory, as suggested by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), it would be better to appoint a commission such as the international frontier commission, for instance.
That commission comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. It has one representative from Canada and one from the United States.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO STUDY LABRADOR LINE
speechtext: What will the United States be doing there?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE TO STUDY LABRADOR LINE
speechtext:
I would ask the hon. member to wait a moment.
That commission is concerned especially with the boundary between Canada and the United States. It does not deal with the boundaries between the provinces of the federal territories.
However, there are other commissions. For instance, the general surveyor of Canada is often called upon to determine, on the spot, the boundary lines between various provinces or the common boundary between the federal territories and the provinces. That is how ad hoc commissions are set up in each case.
The general surveyor of Canada has been asked to help mark the boundaries between British Columbia and Alberta, between Alberta and Saskatchewan, between Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and between Ontario and Manitoba. In each of these cases, a tripartite commission was set up, with a representative of each of the provinces involved and one of the federal government, which in such cases is always the general surveyor of Canada.
In other cases, where boundaries between a province and a federal territory are involved, it is a bipartite commission. That was the case of British Columbia and Yukon, of Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories, as well as of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories.
The cost of marking those boundaries is generally divided in two equal shares in the case of a bipartite commission.
When tripartite commissions were established, that is, when two provinces wanted to settle their boundary problems by asking the federal government to participate, in

Quebec-Newfoundland Boundary some instances, the federal government paid a certain amount; in some cases also, many years ago, the federal government did not contribute anything, but acted as arbitrator.
In the case of the frontier between Manitoba and Saskatchewan, the federal government recently took part in the work involved and paid one third of the total cost, the two provinces concerned paying one third each.
This participation by the federal government has never been imposed by the general surveyor of Canada; in other words, the federal government waits for a formal invitation before undertaking any such work.
As far as Quebec is concerned, the problem of the Labrador frontier is not the only one creating a conflict. The question of the islands in lake St. Francois is still to be settled definitely between Ontario and Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I am under the impression that some federal ministers of mines and technical surveys have in the past offered to help the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to solve this problem and I do not believe that either the federal government, Quebec or Ontario have received any answer in that respect.
As far as the Quebec-Labrador boundary is concerned, the federal government has never been invited to participate in any way in that delimitation. On the maps issued by the federal government, the boundary line indicated is that of the level of the lands, according to a judgment rendered in 1927 by the London privy council. On the maps issued by the province of Quebec, that boundary is never shown-at least on those issued during the last 20 or 30 years-and in the corner of the map, we usually find that reference:
The boundary line between Quebec and Newfoundland is not shown on that map, with good reason.
I believe that footnote was added on the maps published by the province of Quebec at the special request of the former premier, Hon. Maurice Duplessis.
If you keep to the decision rendered by the privy council in London in 1927, you would, of course, have to determine on the spot the exact position of that boundary line between what is commonly called Labrador and Quebec. You could then proceed according to one of the following methods:
First, the governments of Quebec and Newfoundland could each appoint a commissioner and agree beforehand to be bound by their findings. In the event of conflict concerning certain points of the boundary, they could refer the question to a consultant or an arbitrator who would be neither from Quebec nor from Newfoundland. This consultant could be a recognized firm of engineers and surveyors, or the surveyor general of Canada.


Second, an independent organization in Quebec or Newfoundland could simply be asked to do the work.
Third, a three-member commission could be created which would include a representative of the province of Quebec, one of Newfoundland and a third one from the federal government. As I say, that is how most provinces proceeded.
Even though I have no idea how much it would cost, I should like to say that modern land-surveying techniques would make it easy to draw a line in the territory concerned. Satisfactory results could be achieved by means of aerial photography and photographic surveying.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must assure the house that we have no intention of taking something away from Newfoundland to give it to Quebec or vice-versa. We just want a commission constituted as I have just indicated, to determine once and for all the boundaries of those two provinces which contribute so much to the economy of the whole country.
The boundary line between those two provinces has, as I said, often been mentioned. I have travelled along those frontiers on many occasions, and I have never seen any official boundary line.
If we refer to the revised statutes of 1952, chapter 11-

The British North America Act, 1871, 34-35 Victoria chapter 28, an act respecting the establishment of provinces in the Dominion of Canada, section 3:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province of the said dominion, increase, diminish or otherwise alter the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed by the said legislature, and may, with the like consent, make provision respecting the effect and operation of any such increase or diminution or alteration of territory in relation to any province affected thereby.

As it is getting late, I again suggest that a commission similar to the one I mentioned a moment ago be set up to determine once and for all the boundary line between those two very important provinces.
